tast: Kill test bundles and related processes. Update test runners to create a new session for each bundle and kill all processes in the session (including processes started by tests) after the bundle exits. Also kill the session if the read end of stdout is closed while tests are running, as this typically indicates that the SSH connection was dropped. Otherwise, the processes can hang around forever. chromeos-chrome: Use compressed binary profiles Clang has grown support for a special type of AFDO profile called a 'compressed binary' profile. This profile format should be functionally identical to our current binary profiles, but allows for lazy loading of function profiles. Given that the incredible majority of TUs should only contain a very small subset of functions represented in the AFDO file, this is expected to save a large amount of RAM and CPU per TU. In practice, given 100 arbitrarily selected C++ compilations with AFDO enabled in Chrome -- I literally just grepped a build log of `ninja -v` and cleaned it up a bit -- we see: Old profile; Max wall-time: 3.29s Average wall-time: 1.055s Min wall-time: 0.84s Max RSS: 578,572KB Average RSS: 486,437KB Min RSS: 463,236KB New profile: Max wall-time: 2.51s Average wall time: 0.260s Min wall-time: 0.05s Max RSS: 158,236KB Average RSS: 64,629KB Min RSS: 40,828KB This is a reduction of ~800ms of CPU and 421.8MB of RAM per TU on average. This reduction should be roughly constant per TU (wall-time reduction for the max wall-times was ~780ms, and memory reduction for the maximum RSSes was 420,296KB), with larger TUs seeing slightly less reduction. Percentage savings are not presented here, since the majority of these randomly-selected compilations were small and quick. I suspect that trying to generalize savings percentages would be over-optimistic. Chrome has many 'heavier' compilations that take hundreds of MB of RAM and seconds of CPU without AFDO, and my fear is that this random set of compilations didn't have a representatively large sample of those. The point was just to show that the savings from lazy loading profiles is roughly constant, and it does appear to be. BUG=None TEST=Built Chrome with both 'regular' and 'compressed binary' profiles. They were bitwise identical. Change-Id: Ibff4845b1ac61b2d23cf6ae8cf8fb1a6524a5935 Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1533248 Commit-Ready: George Burgess <gbiv@chromium.org> Tested-by: George Burgess <gbiv@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Manoj Gupta <manojgupta@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Luis Lozano <llozano@chromium.org> Reviewed-by: Mike Frysinger <vapier@chromium.org>

If a device exceeds 16 collections (HID_DEFAULT_NUM_COLLECTIONS), the array to store the collections is reallocated, the pointer to the parent collection becomes invalid. Add i2c-pseudo Linux kernel module. This Linux kernel module provides I2C adapters that can be backed by userspace programs. This allows for userspace implementations of functionality such as tunneling I2C through another communication channel to a remote I2C bus. BRANCH=none BUG=b:79684405 TEST=Used i2c-tools CLI to i2c-dev to issue I2C queries, and Python interactive interpreter as the I2C pseudo adapter controller. The i2c-pseudo module correctly proxied write, read, write+read, and multi-byte reads through the controller character device, and it correctly proxied back the responses from the character device, including the specific byte values read. Later, I implemented an I2C pseudo controller in Servod and used it to flash an ITE EC over I2C using both Servo Micro and Suzy-Q. Change-Id: Idda764e56b9e9d577302b59286e873291ea36d25 Signed-off-by: Matthew Blecker <matthewb@chromium.org> Reviewed-on: https://chromium-review.googlesource.com/1250029 Reviewed-by: Nick Sanders <nsanders@chromium.org>

FROMGIT: ARM: dts: rockchip: Add device tree for rk3288-veyron-mighty Mighty is basically the same Chromebook as Jaq but it has a full-sized SD slot and some different (slightly more rugged) plastics around it. Like Jaq, Mighty may show up with various different brandings but all of them have the same board inside. In the downstream kernel Mighty and Jaq share a "dtsi" and Mighty just adds the SD write protect (needed for a full-sized SD slot).
